01 · Overview

Ticket pricing shouldn't
feel like a plot twist

For years, the live events industry has run on a "drip pricing" playbook. You see a tempting base price upfront, then the fees sneak in later at checkout like an uninvited guest. It is common across the whole category, but it quietly torches trust at the exact moment that matters most: the half second before someone hits "Place Order."

At TicketNetwork, this stopped being a someday problem and became a now problem. FTC scrutiny around pricing transparency was heating up, and the business genuinely needed to lift conversion and stop the bleeding at checkout. So I treated this as a chance to rethink how price shows up across the entire journey, turning a fragmented, slightly sneaky flow into something clear, predictable, and honestly kind of refreshing.

💡 Here is the spicy part: showing people the real price upfront made stakeholders genuinely nervous. The worry was that we would look pricier than competitors still hiding their fees. My job was to prove that honesty could lift conversion instead of tanking it, and to prove it with data rather than vibes.
💸

Sticker shock at checkout

Users browsed happily on Maps and the Ticket List based on the base price they saw. Then fees landed at checkout, the total jumped, and the mood went from "let's go" to "wait, what." That gap is where they bailed.

🔀

Inconsistent pricing language

"Estimated Subtotal" here, "Price Per Ticket" there, all used interchangeably across surfaces. Each tiny mismatch was harmless on its own, but together they compounded into real confusion about what the price actually was.

📉

Drop-off at the worst possible moment

Funnel data kept telling the same story: a sharp abandonment spike the instant fees appeared. That is the highest intent moment in the whole journey, and we were losing people right at the finish line.

⚖️

Compliance pressure building

FTC guidance on drip pricing was evolving fast. That made transparency both a risk to manage and an opportunity to grab. Solving it proactively meant getting ahead of regulation and ahead of competitors at the same time.

02 · Discovery

A pricing problem in disguise.
Actually a trust problem.

Before I designed a single pixel, I wanted to know why pricing felt broken in the first place. So I teamed up with product and went spelunking through the checkout funnel data and drop-off patterns, zeroing in on where our highest intent users were quietly giving up.

This was never really a pricing issue. It was a trust issue wearing a pricing costume. Every mismatch between Maps, Ticket List, and Checkout chipped away at confidence a little more.

User flow audit: Where trust breaks, before all-in pricing

I went screen by screen across Maps, then Ticket List, then Checkout, tracing exactly how pricing was displayed, labeled, and quietly transformed at each step. What I found was subtle but kind of damning: we were not just inconsistent, we were breaking user expectations over and over. A price would look one way on Maps, shift slightly in the list view, then get relabeled at checkout. Nothing was technically broken, yet the whole thing left users with this low hum of wait, am I missing something?

🔍 Key insight: once I mapped every inconsistency across the full journey, I could not unsee it. I catalogued every label mismatch, pressure tested the language, and built a clear picture of exactly where trust broke and why.

The experience users actually had: pricing as a jump scare

The mobile checkout flow made the core problem impossible to miss. The order summary opens with just the ticket cost showing. Fees and the real total only appear once you expand the section, way too late in the journey.

Mobile viewport scroll: Checkout experience, before all-in pricing
Scrolling the existing mobile checkout. Fees only show up after you expand "MORE DETAILS," which lands the sticker shock late in the flow, right when commitment is highest.
⚠️ The gap between the "base" price and the real total was only revealed at the most critical moment, right before payment. That is exactly where users walked.
03 · Process

Mobile-first, then
scaled to desktop

Instead of treating each page as its own little island, I approached pricing as one connected experience. I mapped the full journey from Discovery to Selection to Checkout, then pinpointed where it cracked: where users formed price expectations, where those expectations got rewritten, and where the friction turned into drop-off.

📱 I designed mobile first, on purpose. Mobile checkout exposed the problem most brutally, because limited screen space forces you to decide what truly earns a spot by default. Nail the hardest canvas first and desktop becomes a scale-up, not a redo.

Research

Partnered with product to dig into the checkout funnel data, and found a consistent drop-off spike the moment fees were introduced. Then I went screen by screen across Maps, Ticket List, and Checkout, cataloguing every label, every price display, and every point of inconsistency along the way.

Reframing: pricing system, not pricing UI
Rather than nudging visuals on individual pages, I zoomed out and rethought the system. How the redesigned system connected the dots

With the audit done and the system approach locked, I mapped how all-in pricing would flow across all three surfaces. The goal was simple to say and hard to earn: the price expectation a user forms on Maps gets honoured all the way through to checkout, no surprises, no fine print reveal.

Redesigned flow: All-In Pricing, one consistent signal from Maps to Ticket List to Checkout
04 · Solution

What you see upfront is accurate.
What's behind it is always one tap away.

I introduced an All-In Pricing experience that surfaces the true ticket cost, fees included, right on Maps and the Ticket List. No more price jump at checkout. What you see while browsing is what you actually pay, full stop.

⚡ The principle I kept coming back to: show the real price by default, but hand users the controls for detail. Collapsible breakdowns meant the default view stayed calm and uncluttered, while the full math was always just one tap away for the people who want it.

Mobile-first: All-In collapsed and expanded states

On mobile I designed two states for the order summary. A clean collapsed view shows the all-in total by default, and a full breakdown sits one caret tap away. Users get instant clarity without being forced to chew through every line item before they are ready.

Mobile solution: All-In pricing, collapsed and expanded states
Collapsed state: Order summary leads with the all-in ticket price. The "MORE DETAILS" caret invites a tap, but the number that matters is already right there.
Expanded state: One tap reveals the full breakdown of Subtotal, Service Fee, Delivery, and Taxes, with a clear Total anchored at the bottom. Full transparency, zero homework.

Where transparency actually starts: the Maps list

As the work unfolded, one insight reframed everything: the real entry point for pricing transparency is not checkout, it is the Maps ticket list. That is where users form their price expectations in the first place. So I pushed the all-in system upstream and added "Fees Included" copy to every ticket item in the Maps view. Now people see fee-inclusive pricing the second they start browsing sections, before they have even picked a seat.

💡 The unlock: if transparency starts at discovery, there is no expectation gap left to awkwardly close at checkout. The entire downstream flow gets easier the moment the first number a user sees is the honest one.
Maps ticket list: "Fees Included" copy on every listing, transparency right at discovery
Every ticket listing now carries "Fees Included," so users know exactly what they are paying from the very first thing they see.

Key design decisions

All-in price displayed by default

The total cost, fees included, shows on Maps and the Ticket List. Users form an accurate price expectation before they ever reach checkout, which deletes the fee-shock moment entirely.

Standardised labels across surfaces

"Price Per Ticket" and "Subtotal" got standardised and used consistently across Maps, Ticket List, and Checkout, killing the slow drip of confusion that label drift had been causing.

Collapsible breakdown via caret

Anyone who wants the full breakdown gets it in a single tap. The default stays clean and clear, the detail layer is always available but never forced, and users keep control without the cognitive tax.

Sticky header with pricing context

As users scroll through checkout, a sticky header keeps the price in view, so nobody loses the thread of what they are paying no matter how deep they are in the form.

05 · The part that didn't go to plan

Two moments where this
almost went sideways

Case studies love to read like a clean arc from problem to applause. This one had teeth. The two hardest moments were not design problems at all, they were a nervous stakeholder room and a brief that kept trying to grow legs. Here is what actually happened and how I handled it.

😬 The pushback

"This is going to make us look more expensive than everyone else."

Leadership was genuinely worried that putting the all-in number on Maps would make our prices look higher than competitors who were still hiding fees until checkout. On a side-by-side listing page, a $487 honest total can absolutely lose to a $396 mirage. That fear was not irrational, and I was not going to win it with a manifesto about transparency in a conference room.

✅ How I handled it

I stopped arguing and turned it into a testable bet.

Instead of trying to win the opinion war, I reframed the whole thing as a hypothesis: if expectation matches reality, more high-intent users finish checkout, even if the upfront number looks bigger. I proposed a phased rollout to site owners with week-over-week conversion as the scoreboard, and I made a point of saying it was reversible. Reversible is the magic word. The moment a scary decision becomes a measurable, undoable experiment, the temperature in the room drops and people let you try.

The bet, made tappable

This is the exact tension I had to make legible to stakeholders, so I am letting you flip it yourself. Toggle between the control (drip pricing, the old way) and the variant (all-in pricing, what I shipped) and watch what happens to the price signal and the trust read. The conversion bar is directional and illustrative of the hypothesis, not a precise per-step metric. The one hard number we measured in the wild lives in the Results section below.

Directional conversion signal
The price you see while browsing is the price you pay. No fee reveal, no flinch at checkout, no "wait, what" moment. This is the version that shipped.
Same seats, same real cost. The only thing that changes is when the truth shows up, and that timing is the entire ballgame.
🪤 The scope creep

"Just fix checkout" quietly became "fix the entire funnel, and maybe filters too."

The brief landed as a checkout problem. But the audit kept dragging me upstream, because the expectation break actually started on Maps. Owning that meant the work wanted to balloon across three surfaces, and once people heard "pricing system" the wishlist started growing: new filter logic, currency handling, a fee-estimator tool. All reasonable. All capable of sinking the timeline and the trust I had just earned.

✅ How I handled it

I triaged ruthlessly and sequenced instead of expanding.

I drew a hard line between what fixed the trust break and what was simply nice to have. The trust break needed exactly three things shipped together: all-in price on Maps, standardised labels, and the collapsible breakdown. Everything else went into a clearly written "phase 2" so nobody felt their idea got thrown away, it just got a place in line. I anchored the cut to the one question that settles most scope fights: does this close the expectation gap, yes or no? The estimator and filter work were genuinely good ideas, so I parked them with a paper trail rather than killing them, and protected the launch that actually moved the metric.

🧭 The throughline across both: I traded certainty I could not have for tests and tradeoffs I could defend. A reversible experiment beats a confident opinion, and a sequenced roadmap beats a heroic, doomed mega-launch. Neither moment went my way at first. Both ended up making the work stronger.
06 · Results

Honesty didn't tank revenue.
It actually helped.

By moving all-in pricing earlier in the funnel, we cut the checkout drop-off caused by fee shock and made the whole thing feel a lot less "gotcha." Users understood what they were paying, trusted it more, and made more confident purchase decisions. Turns out treating people like adults is good for business.

07 · Takeaways

What I'd carry
into every project

→
Treat pricing as a system, not a screen
Fixing checkout alone would never have solved the trust problem, because the expectation break started all the way back on Maps. The only way to fix trust was to fix the whole journey. Pricing is a system, and systems demand end-to-end thinking.
→
Mobile-first sharpens decisions
Starting on mobile forced the hardest tradeoffs up front. What truly needs to be visible by default? What can live behind a tap? Those constraints produced cleaner, more intentional patterns, and scaling to desktop was easy because the logic was already bulletproof.
→
Transparency is a conversion strategy
The fear was that showing the full price early would scare users off. The data said the exact opposite. People who understand what they are paying are people who finish the purchase. Honesty, it turns out, is good UX and good business at the same time.
